name: Pyratine-6

card.summary: A topical furfuryladenine (kinetin-related) cream studied for photodamaged skin and rosacea, aimed at smoother, less red skin.
card.note: Evidence consists of small open-label studies.

quick.overview:
Pyratine-6 is a topical furfuryladenine compound, related to kinetin, that was sold in cosmetic and rosacea-care products. It was developed by Senetek.

In small studies it was linked with smoother texture, fewer fine wrinkles, less mottled pigmentation and less redness, which is why it appeals for even, calmer-looking skin.
quick.how: Studies used a lotion or cream applied twice daily for 12 weeks or longer, with changes seen from two to four weeks.
quick.risks: Adverse effects in studies were minimal and transient. Trials were small and open-label.

lead: Pyratine-6 is a topical cosmetic compound in the furfuryladenine family, related to kinetin, which was first isolated from herring sperm DNA and is a cytokinin plant hormone.[4] A related formulation, PRK 124 (Pyratine-XR), was studied for rosacea.[2]

In a 12-week single-arm study of 40 women with photodamaged facial skin, 0.10% Pyratine-6 twice daily improved roughness and moisture by 2 weeks and fine wrinkles, mottled pigmentation and transepidermal water loss by 4 weeks, with reduced erythema.[1]
Open-label rosacea studies showed reductions in redness and lesions.[2][3]

chain: Better barrier and moisture, less redness
angle.text: Studies reported improved texture, reduced fine wrinkles and less redness, which translates to calmer, smoother-looking skin.

paras: Cosmetic use targets photodamage; a rosacea lotion was tested separately.[1][2]
A 12-week study of 40 women found significant improvements in roughness, moisture, fine wrinkles, pigmentation and erythema, with minimal, transient adverse effects.[1]
In a 12-week open-label rosacea study, 21 participants completed treatment; 80 percent showed overall improvement, with reduced erythema, papules, telangiectasia and TEWL.[2]
A 48-week open-label study of 18 subjects reported a mean 44 percent reduction in erythema and 89 percent reduction in inflammatory lesions.[3] These studies lacked control groups.
